# vpn0wn WireGuard provisioning scripts

Last updated: 2026-10-17 (Europe/Paris).

These vpn0wn-owned Bash commands adapt the [pinned upstream reference](../UPSTREAM.md) into a non-interactive server surface. Android uses these scripts rather than the upstream interactive installer. Concrete Android SSH transport and read-only Detect/Plan/manual-status source wiring exist. Confirmed fresh installation, user creation/encrypted retention and authenticated profile-access source are delivered through [PRs #201](https://github.com/novakin/vpn0wn-android/pull/201), [#202](https://github.com/novakin/vpn0wn-android/pull/202) and [#203](https://github.com/novakin/vpn0wn-android/pull/203). Android/live runtime acceptance and remaining mutation UI stay open under #143. The #196 snapshot/codec foundation is delivered through merged [PR #204](https://github.com/novakin/vpn0wn-android/pull/204); the separate fresh-destination restore source is delivered through merged [PR #205](https://github.com/novakin/vpn0wn-android/pull/205), after independent ultra review and final-head CI. A separate [private encrypted-export candidate](../../../docs/backend-contracts.md#private-encrypted-server-export-candidate--196) now wires the first file path. Its [scoped API34 writer controls](../../../docs/reviews/2026-10-17-native-backup-export-acceptance.md) pass UI retirement/drain and independent file recovery at unchanged format/KDF; [PR #226](https://github.com/novakin/vpn0wn-android/pull/226) delivered the experimental export source after final-head review/checks; restore UI remains unwired.

This guide describes the C2–C4 source repairs and offline proof. Confirmation does not establish ownership; successful JSON does not establish traffic or handshake health. [Backend contracts](../../../docs/backend-contracts.md#provisioning-command-surface) owns strict Android schemas, safe error categories and health meaning; [the plan](../../../docs/improvement-plan.md#codebase-actions) tracks delivery and remaining work.

## Scope and defaults

Install/plan support Ubuntu/Debian and apt. Default state is `wg0` under `/etc/wireguard`, with metadata under `/etc/wireguard/tunnl`. Shared `WG_IFACE`, `WG_DIR`, `WG_CONF` and `TUNNL_DIR` environment overrides exist. `FORWARD_CONF` defaults to `/etc/sysctl.d/99-tunnl-wireguard-forward.conf`; `WG_LOCK_FILE` and `WG_HOST_LOCK_FILE` select native lock paths. Overrides support private offline fixtures; alternate live interfaces/platforms have not been validated. Allocation supports IPv4 `.0/24` pools, IPv4 client default routes and iptables NAT.

Plan/install require a single hostname/IPv4 token or bracketed IPv6 endpoint and default to UDP `51820`, CIDR `10.8.0.0/24` and DNS `1.1.1.1, 1.0.0.1`. Ports are bounded decimal values. DNS accepts comma-separated address/search-domain tokens; client AllowedIPs accepts comma-separated IPv4/IPv6 CIDRs. Controls, newlines, empty tokens and config-section/hook injection are rejected. IPv6 checks are lexical, not a full address parser or resolver. Install uses configured apt repositories for `wireguard`, `iptables` and `qrencode`.

## Current command behavior

| Command | Source-observed result and limitation |
| --- | --- |
| `detect.sh` | Reports distro, tools/firewall hints, config/package presence and forwarding. Endpoint comes from config metadata, not external public-IP discovery. |
| `plan.sh` | Validates endpoint, port, CIDR, DNS and OS, then emits static install steps and an overwrite flag. Accepts the shared request's `--force` without changing this advisory result. It changes no state and does not prove root access, ownership or install feasibility. |
| `install.sh` | Requires root and ownership, stages config, enables/restarts the unit and checks service, server key, port, address and peer state. Forced reinstall stops the old unit with its old config/hooks before replacement. Existing config fails without `--force`; force never bypasses ownership. |
| `add-peer.sh` | Locks allocation/read/write/apply, accepts optional `--expected-server-public-key`, rejects duplicate names or ambiguous markers, and returns a secret-bearing profile after disk/runtime postconditions. A supplied server key must match configured identity and any running interface before mutation admission. |
| `remove-peer.sh` | Accepts `--name`, optional `--expected-public-key` and optional `--expected-server-public-key`; removes one ordered, unambiguous block and checks disk/live peer removal. Absent names fail. Success emits `name`, `publicKey`, `removed:true` and `revoked:false`. |
| `revoke-peer.sh` | Accepts name/client-key and optional server-key guards. Optional `--operation-id` selects a UUID-correlated no-clobber archive; omission retains the legacy six-character suffix. Validates and flushes the original private block before removal under the same lock. Success additionally includes `archiveName` and nullable `operationId`. History includes PSK/server metadata, not the full client profile. |
| `sync-status.sh` | Requires root, managed regular config and unambiguous markers; takes the existing interface lock before returning saved peer metadata, `serverPublicKey`, nullable actual `runtimePeerPublicKeys` and complete `configuredPeerPublicKeys` and observed runtime handshake/transfer counters. The canonical public key derives from configured private identity; running interfaces must expose the same public identity. Failed derivation, unobservable runtime or live/configured identity drift returns a null key. Shared `observe_runtime` checks native interface presence: true/false/null for running/stopped/unobservable. Missing/failed dump, missing rows and invalid/out-of-range counters produce null, not zero. Interface presence is independent of systemd activity and does not prove connectivity. |
| `backup.sh` | Returns snapshot version 1 with exact server config, UTC capture date and every supported retained revoked body under the interface lock. Existing interface/config/count fields remain; ownership, safe regular files, valid text and bounded encoded output are required. It writes no encrypted file. Protect the secret-bearing result; [snapshot schema](../../../docs/backend-contracts.md#managed-server-snapshot--196) owns fields and limits. |
| `restore.sh` | Source-only fresh `wg0` restore requiring `--input`, `--endpoint`, `--port`, `--expected-server-public-key` and `--confirm`. Validates all supported input before mutation, requires installed tools and an absent destination, preserves keys/PSKs/history, regenerates hooks and checks actual runtime/history. No force, package installation, UI or live acceptance; [restore contract](../../../docs/backend-contracts.md#fresh-destination-restore-source--196) owns exact boundaries. |
| `uninstall.sh` | Requires `--confirm` and ownership, writes a unique private backup before stop/disable/delete, and verifies absence. Optional purge refuses other config/live interfaces and checks named package absence. No autoremove runs. Global forwarding stays unchanged; its managed file stays when another interface/config exists. |

## Ownership, locking and recovery

Existing-state mutations require a regular non-symlink config containing the exact existing `# TUNNL_MANAGED 1` marker. Missing config fails peer/uninstall commands. Fresh install and fresh restore source have their separate absent-config admission; restore rejects even an owned existing config. Forwarding replacement/removal accepts only the exact legacy `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` file or its marked equivalent. Config/forwarding checks run before lock/filesystem/service/package effects and are repeated under lock. Fresh install also observes interfaces under lock before state writes/packages and rejects a collision without owned config, even when `wg` is absent. The marker is an ownership convention, not authentication against another root process.

All writers take a stable per-interface `flock` at `/run/lock/tunnl-wireguard-$WG_IFACE.lock`. Install/uninstall/restore first take `/run/lock/tunnl-wireguard-host.lock` for shared host state, then the interface lock. Locks are never deleted by uninstall. Status reads take the same per-interface lock and repeat ownership/peer-marker checks inside it, preventing a cooperating write from splitting config/runtime observations. Backup holds the same interface lock through config and revoked-history acquisition. External tools that bypass these locks remain outside serialization.

Remove/revoke retain the supported legacy operator CLI: omitting `--expected-public-key` selects the current peer by sanitized name. When supplied, the argument must be a nonblank canonical 32-byte WireGuard base64 key. After acquiring the interface lock, the command checks current ownership/markers and compares the selected peer key before recovery snapshots, candidate files, archives or config/runtime writes. A reused name with a different key fails with `peer_identity_mismatch`; absent peers fail with `peer_not_found`. These preflight failures do not start a mutation or carry transaction recovery metadata. Lock-file creation remains part of existing admission. Android always requires/passes the captured public key and exact marker name; it has no unguarded fallback. The disposable integration harness also passes each add response's key and checks the returned mutation key. The Android confirmed removal and correlated revocation flows add durable admission and read-only reconciliation. Client-key rotation remains unavailable.

Add and remove retain their legacy CLI when `--expected-server-public-key` is omitted. A supplied key must be canonical and match the locked configured public identity; when the interface runs, its live key must also match. Drift fails with `server_identity_mismatch`, and an unobservable live identity fails with `runtime_unknown`, before recovery snapshots, add-only client key/PSK generation or config/runtime writes. Status consumers accept older payloads without `serverPublicKey` as identity unavailable; missing or null identity cannot authorize Android create or retained-profile reopen. Status also reads native `wg show wg0 peers` under that lock: successful empty output becomes `[]`, while failed/partial/malformed/duplicate output becomes null. Known stopped interfaces emit `[]`; unobservable state emits null. Missing/null legacy inventory remains unknown to Android. The separate configured inventory reads every `[Peer]` block, including unmarked blocks and ordinary assignment whitespace. Missing/duplicate keys, malformed keys or unsupported sections make that inventory unknown. Named rows alone prove neither complete disk absence nor live absence; Android removal requires known absence from both inventories. Neither the lock nor a public identity check serializes external tools that bypass this lock.

Private recovery directories live on the config filesystem with mode 0700; configs, runtime snapshots, backups and revoke archives use 0600. Candidates pass checked `wg-quick strip` before atomic rename. A running peer mutation uses `wg syncconf`, falls back to restart on command failure, then checks server key/port and exact peer keys/routes/PSKs. A stopped interface receives persistent config only and must remain absent; this is not live revocation proof. Strip extracts wg-quick fields; it is not a complete native validator for a stopped interface.

Write/apply/stop/disable/postcondition failures attempt to restore old disk/native runtime and, for install/uninstall/restore, service state. Runtime snapshots preserve pre-existing live state independently of saved config. Restore source additionally recovers its prior absent/empty revoked history and observed live forwarding value. Peer recovery does not snapshot or verify prior systemd unit state; restart fallback can change unit activity for a manually started interface. Failure JSON reports `recovery` as `unchanged`, `restored` or `incomplete`; incomplete recovery retains private files at `recoveryPath`. An uninstall backup is retained and reported as `artifact` even on failure. Recovery never includes raw tool diagnostics or config payloads.

Package installation/purge and global forwarding enable are not an OS transaction. After attempted package changes, failure explicitly warns that those effects may remain. Partial purge can leave tools unavailable and recovery incomplete; retain the backup and inspect state before retrying. Uninstall success with purge requires named packages absent/not-installed, not merely residual `config-files` status. Existing unrelated packages are not autoremoved.

After operation postconditions and archive publication commit, cleanup does not roll back using partially deleted snapshots. Success includes `cleanupPath`: empty when cleanup completed, otherwise the private residue needing operator inspection/removal. Signals during mutation trigger recovery where Bash can handle them; SIGKILL, host loss and a lost remote response still require reconciliation.

Correlated revocation validates and flushes the original archive before destructive apply. Complete rollback removes only its owned archive; incomplete recovery retains both archive and private recovery material. `sync-status.sh` publishes only complete validated public archive metadata or null, never private bodies/PSKs. Plain, six-character and UUID archive names retain their bounded snapshot/restore validation; [the revoke contract](../../../docs/backend-contracts.md#correlated-user-revocation--143) owns correlation and read-only settlement. A retained archive alone does not establish peer absence.

## Fresh-destination restore source

The separate [local encrypted-backup inspection candidate](../../../docs/backend-contracts.md#local-encrypted-backup-inspection--196) reads a selected Android document through authentication/password and a bounded decoder to a safe summary. It invokes no SSH/server command and changes no saved record. Its acceptance remains separate from privileged restore grammar, destination admission and live restoration; the summary is not a restore plan.

`restore.sh` requires root, supported Ubuntu/Debian and already installed WireGuard/network tools; it makes no apt/package changes. Input is exactly regular `server.conf` plus a regular `revoked/` directory of supported snapshot basenames. Empty lines are allowed, but all nonempty fields must match the ordered LF-only managed grammar. CR, tabs, controls, unknown directives/comments, arbitrary hooks and reordered fields fail before destination mutation. Keys are canonical; active peers have unique names/keys/current-pool `.2–.254/32` addresses. Historical revoked blocks may retain prior subnets and reused names/addresses, with optional PSK absence, but cannot contain an active peer key. Complete revoked bytes survive restoration; supported NAT hooks are regenerated rather than replayed.

The supplied expected server public key must match the restored private key. Destination checks reject existing config, nonempty history, unsafe paths, any existing `wg0` interface/link and a selected UDP-port holder. Retained `WG_DIR` must be root-owned without group/other write bits, and retained `TUNNL_DIR` must be exactly root-owned `0700`; rejection preserves their modes. Any overlapping IPv4 address prefix, including broader `noprefixroute` addresses, or contained/covering route across all tables returns `subnet_in_use`. Ordinary unicast default routing is allowed; typed deny default routes conflict. Failed/malformed observations remain `runtime_unknown`. Admission repeats under host-then-interface locks. Checked postconditions cover actual key/port, peer keys/routes/PSKs, address, service and exact history readback. [Scoped source checks](../../../docs/qa-test-plan.md#fresh-destination-restore-controls--196) pass at their recorded uncommitted scope; subsequent source delivery through [PR #205](https://github.com/novakin/vpn0wn-android/pull/205) has its own final-head independent review and CI. Same-host replacement, preview/client endpoint updates, file/UI workflow, live SSH/restore/traffic and release remain separate #196 work. [The contract](../../../docs/backend-contracts.md#fresh-destination-restore-source--196) owns limits, receipts and recovery.

## Output and safety boundaries

Normal responses and explicit failures use JSON on stdout. Mutating-command diagnostics omit raw package/tool output. Value-taking options in plan/install/peer commands reject missing values. Backup checks root, ownership, `iconv`, complete NUL-delimited directory enumeration, reads and bounds before publishing one complete result; NUL in file contents is unsupported because Bash cannot retain it. Enumeration failure cannot become empty revocation history. Shared JSON escaping now preserves other control characters, including CR. Detect/sync and pre-transaction shell failures are not a uniformly guarded error protocol. Commands are non-interactive but not uniformly idempotent: duplicate add, absent remove and existing install can fail.

Never log or publish generated configs, backup payloads, private keys or PSKs. Shell-quoted arguments do not validate WireGuard config content. No script manages SSH configuration or intentionally edits SSH port rules; this is not a guarantee about all host firewall/package effects.

Android consumes agreed C4 JSON/health contracts. C9 now checks exact saved/live peer and uninstall/package postconditions with payload-free failures and owned cleanup; see [harness proof](../../../docs/development.md#c9-offline-harness-postconditions--2026-10-09). Real SSH/UI integration (C11–C12) remains unfinished. Offline script/harness proof does not establish real-server behavior.

## Verification

Run [the offline suite](../../../scripts/tests/provisioning_safety_test.sh) through an unprivileged Linux user namespace; see [C2–C3 evidence](../../../docs/development.md#c2c3-offline-provisioning-safety--2026-10-06) and [C4 contract evidence](../../../docs/development.md#c4-provisioning-contracts-and-observed-health--2026-10-06). Fixtures use synthetic keys, private temporary files and fake privileged commands. The suite compares actual normalized script responses to committed synthetic JSON consumed by JVM tests. Syntax alone does not establish mutation safety. C9 adds standard-library injected offline harness controls; the [disposable VPS harness](../../../docs/qa-test-plan.md#disposable-vps-integration-use-case) still needs explicit target authorization for a live run. No APK, SSH or live VPN proof was run for this change.
